text: Here are two clips of the same flat landscape. In one, the music is quick and bright. In the other, it's slow and low. One sky is yellow, the other blue-gray. Pick which sky goes with which music, and keep an eye on the strip at the bottom, which has two scales, happy to sad and strong to weak, because we'll need them. I'm Tanmay Kulkarni in for Humanitarian's AI. If you put the yellow sky on the quick tune, you picked the way most listeners do in two different countries. Here's the odd part, though. Nothing in a yellow sky sounds quick, so what are people actually matching? In 2013, Stephen Palmer and colleagues

At Berkeley played 18 pieces of orchestral music by Bach, Mozart, and Brahms, 50 seconds each. Some were slow, some medium, some fast, and major and minor. About 97 people in the United States and in Mexico listened. For each piece, they picked the five colors that fit best from a set of 37, and the five that fit worst. In both countries, quick major music drew lighter, more saturated yellower colors. Slow minor music drew darker, grayer, bluer ones. Here's what they think is underneath. People also rated every piece and every color on feelings, happy, sad, strong, weak, and more. Rate the music, rate the colors it drew, and the two line up. .97

For happy to sad, .96 for strong to weak. Across all four word pairs, .89 to .99. So, the idea is that color doesn't hear the music. Both carry the same feeling. One honest limit, these are correlations. The authors say so, and they say a direct link isn't ruled out. Run it with the paper's own two examples, Bach's fast dance in F major, rated happy strong. Which colors sit in that corner? The paper says saturated yellow and light yellow. Now, Brahms' slow adagio in C minor, sad, weak, black, dark, grey, dark, cyan. The step in the middle is the rating. The sound never has to touch the color.

Why would color be ready to carry feeling at all? In an essay we read, babies sort colors into categories by about 6 months and name them by about 18. So, the sorting comes before the words. A color can mean something to you before you have a word for it. How far does the match travel? Between the United States and Mexico, very far. The correlations between the two countries ran from 0.8 to 0.97 across the color measures. But, those are two countries in the Americas and the music was Western classical. The authors write that it's unclear for music built on other scales. And the essay we read adds

That color symbols differ. White for purity in much of the West, morning in many Eastern cultures. So, take it as strong, not as a law. Now, put that to work. The essay we read describes how editors set a rhythm of arousal with scene length. Long, calm scenes, short, busy ones. It's rule of thumb is a calm scene of 7 to 12 seconds set against a busy one of 1 to 3. Look at those two strips. Same length of film, very different pulse. It pairs the calm strip with cool colors and the busy one with warm. Pacing has been tested, too, on its own. In 2011, Angeline Lillard and Jennifer

Peterson had 64-year-olds watch a fast cartoon, watch a slower one, or draw for 9 minutes. Right afterwards, the fast group did worse on four tasks of self-control and planning. That test was about pacing, not color. It measured the immediate effect and it was one group of four-year-olds. Here's a case where two things pull against each other. Fast music pulls toward yellow and minor pulls toward blue. The paper played every combination, so fast and minor is in the data. Use the strip fast as strong, minor as sad, so where does fast and minor land? Then answer two more questions about it. Is its color lighter or darker than slow minors? Is it more

Or less saturated than fast majors? Pause here and write down both answers. Here's what the paper's chart shows. Read off its figure for the United States listeners. Fast minor music drew colors lighter, more saturated and yellower than slow minor, and less than fast major. Tempo and mode each moved the colors on their own, and fast minor landed between. If you guessed between, the method held. If you guessed one pole, that's where it needs more than two scales. So, here's the opening again, swapped. The quick tune under the blue-gray sky, the slow tune under the yellow one. It feels wrong, and now you know why. It

Isn't that the colors can't hear. It's that each of them is carrying a feeling, and the feelings don't agree. I'm Taimur Khan Carney in for Humanitarian's AI. The study is Palmer's, and it all began with an essay we read.
